dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own

Good — confirms an internal image-proxy route that fetches external media on behalf of the browser. I now have enough to build the system map. Let me submit the phase 1 proposal.

payload_or_id.description: PostgreSQL database. Sole persistent datastore for the service: users, API keys, sessions, categories, feeds, entries, enclosures, icons, integration settings, and feed-refresh scheduling state (next_check_at, error counters). Every other component either reads/writes it directly or depends on something that does.

net/http server(s) (internal/http/server) that host all HTTP routing for the process: applies shared middleware, mounts the REST API, Fever API, Google Reader API, web UI, health probes, and metrics endpoint, and dispatches on-demand feed refreshes into the feed-refresh worker pool.

REST API v1 (/v1/*), used by third-party clients, mobile apps, and the `client` Go package. Covers feed/category/entry CRUD, manual feed refresh trigger, subscription discovery, OPML import/export, user/API-key management.

Server-rendered web UI (catch-all `/` route), the primary end-user entry point: login (form-based, OAuth2, WebAuthn), feed/entry browsing, manual save-to-integration action, and the built-in image proxy that fetches external media on the browser's behalf.
Fever API compatibility endpoint (/fever/*) allowing third-party Fever-protocol clients to read/manage feeds and entries.
Google Reader API compatibility endpoint (/accounts/ClientLogin, /reader/api/0/*) allowing third-party GReader-protocol clients to authenticate and sync feeds/entries.

Health-probe endpoints (/healthcheck, /liveness, /healthz, /readiness, /readyz) used by orchestrators (Docker, Kubernetes, systemd) to determine process liveness and readiness; the readiness probe pings the database.

Prometheus-format /metrics endpoint (only mounted when METRICS_COLLECTOR is enabled), scraped by an external Prometheus server. Exposes HTTP handler metrics plus the gauges/histograms produced by the metrics-collector worker.
`-healthcheck <url|auto>` CLI invocation: the binary calls out to its own (or a target) health endpoint over HTTP and exits non-zero on failure. Used as the Docker HEALTHCHECK command.

In-process goroutine (internal/cli/scheduler.go feedScheduler) that, on a fixed tick (POLLING_FREQUENCY), queries the database for a batch of feeds whose next_check_at has expired and pushes them as jobs into the feed-refresh worker pool. Only runs when this process has the scheduler service enabled and is not in maintenance mode.

Fixed-size pool of goroutines (internal/worker) consuming feed-refresh jobs from an in-memory channel. For each job it fetches the feed over HTTP, parses it, optionally scrapes full content and fetches favicons, persists new/updated entries, and pushes new entries to enabled third-party integrations. Fed by worker.feed_scheduler and by on-demand refresh requests from the REST API.

In-process goroutine (internal/cli/scheduler.go cleanupScheduler) that, on a fixed tick (CLEANUP_FREQUENCY), removes expired web sessions, archives old read/unread entries, and deletes orphaned feed icons. Only runs when this process has the scheduler service enabled and is not in maintenance mode.

In-process goroutine (internal/metric) that periodically queries the database for gauges (user count, feed count by status, entry count by status, etc.) and exposes them to the /metrics endpoint. Only runs when METRICS_COLLECTOR is enabled.

In-process goroutine started when the process is launched under systemd with a watchdog interval configured: periodically pings the database and, if healthy, notifies systemd's watchdog; also sends the initial readiness notification.

`-migrate` CLI flag (or automatic execution at daemon startup when RUN_MIGRATIONS is set): applies pending SQL schema migrations to the database. Runs before any other startup step and blocks daemon start on failure.

`-refresh-feeds` CLI flag: one-shot batch feed refresh equivalent to worker.feed_scheduler + worker.feed_refresh_pool, run to completion and then exit. Used by deployments that drive feed refresh from an external cron instead of the built-in scheduler.

`-run-cleanup-tasks` CLI flag: one-shot equivalent of worker.cleanup_scheduler, run to completion and then exit. Used by deployments that drive cleanup from an external cron instead of the built-in scheduler.

Interactive/rare one-off CLI administrative commands run directly by an operator: -create-admin, -reset-password, -flush-sessions, -export-user-feeds, -reset-feed-errors, -reset-feed-next-check-at. All are synchronous, exit immediately after completion, and act only on the database.

Arbitrary, user-subscribed external RSS/Atom/JSON/RDF feed servers, polled over HTTP(S) by the fetcher (internal/reader/fetcher). Fully outside operator control: availability, latency, TLS validity, and response format vary per feed and per host.
Origin websites of feed entries, fetched over HTTP(S) for full-content extraction (readability/scraper) when a feed has crawler mode enabled.
Origin websites/favicon URLs fetched over HTTP(S) by the icon checker (internal/reader/icon) when creating a feed or when a feed icon is missing.
External OAuth2/OIDC identity providers (Google, and any generic OIDC provider configured via OAUTH2_OIDC_*) used for user authentication in the web UI.

Collection of 25+ user-configured third-party bookmarking, read-later, and notification/webhook services (e.g. Pinboard, Wallabag, Instapaper, Notion, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Matrix, ntfy, Pushover, generic webhook, and more) that entries are pushed to on manual save and/or on new-entry arrival, called from internal/integration.
Optional outbound HTTP/SOCKS proxy or proxy-rotation pool (HTTP_CLIENT_PROXY / proxyrotator) used when fetching feeds or scraped content, either application-wide or per-feed.
Optional external RSS-Bridge instance queried during subscription discovery to generate a feed for websites that do not natively expose one.
Optional systemd service manager on the host, used for readiness (sd_notify READY=1) and watchdog (WATCHDOG=1) notifications when the process is launched with a systemd notify socket.

event.text:
All 26 system-map entries were accepted in the first batch (confirmed — a duplicate `add` for `sm-postgresql` was rejected, proving it already exists).

## Phase 1 — System Map: submitted

I mapped Miniflux (Go RSS/Atom reader service) into 26 `system_components`:

**Datastore (1)**: PostgreSQL — the sole persistent store; everything else depends on it directly or transitively.

**Service (1)**: the shared HTTP server hosting all routing.

**Entrypoints (8)**: REST API (`/v1`), Web UI, Fever API, Google Reader API, health-probe endpoints, Prometheus `/metrics`, and the CLI `-healthcheck` probe used by container orchestrators.

**Workers (5)**: feed scheduler, feed-refresh worker pool, cleanup scheduler, metrics collector, systemd-watchdog goroutine.

**Jobs (4)**: CLI migrate, CLI batch feed-refresh, CLI cleanup-tasks, and a grouped "admin maintenance" job for the rare interactive commands (create-admin, reset-password, flush-sessions, export-user-feeds, reset-feed-errors, reset-feed-next-check-at).

**External dependencies (7)**: arbitrary external feed sources, content-scraper target sites, favicon source sites, OAuth2/OIDC providers, the 25+ third-party bookmark/notification/webhook integration targets (grouped as one component, individually enumerable later if a failure mode needs it), an optional outbound proxy, an optional RSS-Bridge instance, and optional systemd.

`depends_on` edges capture the real failure-chain shape: e.g. the feed-refresh worker pool is what actually talks to feed sources, scrapers, favicons, integrations, and the proxy — both the built-in scheduler path and the CLI batch-refresh job feed into (or duplicate) that same logic, so a failure there has two distinct triggers worth treating as separate early-detection points in phase 2.

Ready for your review. Let me know if you want any component split further (e.g. individual integration providers), merged, or reclassified before we move into phase 2 (failure modes).

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.title: Daemon process down / unreachable
payload_or_id.description: The miniflux process is not running, has crashed, failed to start, or is hung so badly the Prometheus scrape target and every HTTP entrypoint are unreachable. Every entrypoint (REST API, web UI, Fever API, Google Reader API, health probes) is unavailable at once -- this is the ultimate user-visible failure for a total outage.

payload_or_id.title: Unhandled panic crashes the whole process
payload_or_id.description: An unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the entire process, since Go does not isolate panics between goroutines without an explicit recover(). Two concrete known-risk sources in this codebase: (1) feed/content parsing on a malformed upstream response, and (2) the bare `go integration.PushEntries(...)` call in the feed-refresh handler, which runs outside net/http's per-request panic recovery entirely.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Indistinguishable from outside once it has already caused fm-daemon-process-down (scrape-target-down), which already pages; whether a given crash was this vs. an OOM kill vs. a runtime fatal error is established from process exit logs during incident response, not from a separate metric.

payload_or_id.title: Out-of-memory condition
payload_or_id.description: Process memory grows until the OS/container OOM-killer terminates it, or the Go runtime itself fails to allocate. Plausible causes: very large feed/scrape response bodies, a burst of concurrently refreshing feeds, or a goroutine/memory leak.

payload_or_id.title: Startup precondition failure (exits before serving)
payload_or_id.description: The daemon exits immediately at startup, before serving any traffic, due to: invalid configuration (config validation), inability to open the configured log file, failure to generate the embedded UI/binary/stylesheet/JS bundles, HTTP listener bind failure or TLS certificate load failure, database connection pool creation failure, database ping failure, SQL migration failure (-migrate or automatic RUN_MIGRATIONS), or a schema-version mismatch when RUN_MIGRATIONS is disabled.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Collapses into fm-daemon-process-down (scrape-target-down) from the outside; a repeatedly failing startup shows up as an orchestrator crash-loop, which is the right layer to alert on restart churn (e.g. Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff / container restart-count) rather than duplicating it with an app-level metric for a process that, by definition, never reaches the point of emitting one.

payload_or_id.title: Database connection failure at runtime
payload_or_id.description: The application cannot open or maintain connections to PostgreSQL after having started successfully: network partition, DB host down or restarting, credentials/DSN rotated without updating DATABASE_URL, the DB server out of connection slots, or a TLS handshake failure. Distinct from fm-startup-precondition-failure, which happens before the daemon ever starts serving.

payload_or_id.title: Database connection pool exhaustion
payload_or_id.description: All connections in the pool are checked out and further requests queue or time out waiting for a free connection -- caused by a spike in concurrent request/worker load, a slow-query regression, or DATABASE_MAX_CONNS set too low for the deployment's concurrency.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated 5xx error rate across HTTP entrypoints
payload_or_id.description: An elevated rate of 5xx responses across the REST API, web UI, Fever API, or Google Reader API -- users see failed page loads, failed syncs, or failed API calls.

payload_or_id.title: Per-request handler panic (recovered)
payload_or_id.description: A panic inside an HTTP handler goroutine (e.g. a nil-pointer bug in template rendering or JSON encoding) is caught by net/http's per-connection recover(), which logs the panic and closes that connection -- the process keeps running but the requesting client sees a broken or empty response.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated HTTP request latency
payload_or_id.description: Page loads, API calls, or sync requests become slow (but still eventually succeed) across one or more HTTP entrypoints.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated login/authentication failure rate
payload_or_id.description: A systemic spike in failures across any login path (form password, API key, HTTP basic auth used by Fever/Google-Reader/metrics, OAuth2/OIDC, WebAuthn) beyond the normal background rate of typos and expired credentials -- e.g. a bad deploy breaking password verification, a DB users-table issue, or clock skew invalidating tokens.

payload_or_id.title: Outbound network egress degraded
payload_or_id.description: The application's outbound network path to the public internet is broken or badly degraded: DNS resolution failing, an egress firewall/NAT/routing issue, or the host's IP being widely rate-limited/blocked by upstream sites. Affects feed fetching, content scraping, favicon fetching, third-party integrations, and RSS-Bridge discovery simultaneously, since they all share the same outbound HTTP client path.

payload_or_id.title: Configured outbound proxy unavailable
payload_or_id.description: The optional configured outbound HTTP/SOCKS proxy, or one entry in the rotation pool, is unreachable, refuses connections, or returns errors -- breaking fetches for every feed/request routed through it, even while general egress is otherwise healthy.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated feed-refresh failure rate
payload_or_id.description: An elevated rate of feed-refresh failures across many feeds/users: fetch errors, timeouts, unexpected HTTP status or feed format, or repeated rate-limiting (429) responses. A small baseline of individual feed failures is expected (dead blogs, misconfigured feeds); this is about a systemic spike, which shows up to users as feed content going stale and unread counts no longer updating.

payload_or_id.title: Feed refresh has stopped entirely
payload_or_id.description: The feed-scheduler tick loop or the feed-refresh worker pool stops making progress entirely -- the scheduler goroutine has exited/deadlocked, or every worker is permanently blocked (e.g. on a hung DB query or a feed fetch with no effective timeout). Unlike a fetch-error spike, entries simply never advance for any feed, indefinitely.

payload_or_id.title: Feed-refresh worker pool saturated
payload_or_id.description: All feed-refresh worker-pool goroutines stay busy for an extended period, typically because many feed sources or the content scraper are responding slowly (the HTTP client timeout is the only bound on a single job), so new jobs queue up faster than they drain and refresh falls behind system-wide.

payload_or_id.title: CLI batch job (refresh-feeds / run-cleanup-tasks) failure
payload_or_id.description: The -refresh-feeds or -run-cleanup-tasks one-shot CLI invocation exits with an error, or is killed mid-run by the external cron/orchestrator, before completing its batch.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: These are short-lived processes that typically exit before a pull-based Prometheus scrape can observe them, so app-emitted metrics aren't a workable detection path. Deployments that drive refresh/cleanup from external cron instead of the built-in scheduler should alert on the cron/CLI job's own exit code (job-failure notification, healthchecks.io-style dead-man's-switch, or systemd OnFailure=) rather than through this service's metrics.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated content-scraper failure rate
payload_or_id.description: An elevated rate of failures/timeouts when fetching origin websites for full-content extraction on feeds with crawler mode enabled -- entries fall back to the short feed summary instead of full content.

payload_or_id.title: Feed favicon fetch failure
payload_or_id.description: Fetching a feed's favicon fails, so the feed shows a generic icon instead.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Purely cosmetic -- a missing favicon has no functional impact -- and expected to fluctuate constantly since it depends on the presence of a favicon on arbitrary third-party sites. No operator action follows from it, so it is not worth alerting.

payload_or_id.title: RSS-Bridge subscription discovery failure
payload_or_id.description: The optional external RSS-Bridge instance used during subscription discovery is unreachable or errors, so discovery fails for sites that only expose a feed via RSS-Bridge.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Low-traffic, synchronous path (new-subscription discovery only, not ongoing refresh): the failure surfaces immediately to the user attempting to add the feed, who sees the error directly and can retry -- a strictly faster feedback loop than any background alert, and not worth paging on.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated third-party integration push failure rate
payload_or_id.description: An elevated failure rate when pushing entries to one or more of the 25+ third-party integration targets (Pinboard, Wallabag, Telegram, Discord, Slack, ntfy, generic webhook, etc.) -- could be a single popular provider having an outage, a miniflux-side bug in one integration client, or widespread outbound egress trouble. Users' saved entries or new-entry notifications silently fail to reach their configured service.

payload_or_id.title: Prometheus cannot scrape /metrics
payload_or_id.description: Prometheus cannot successfully scrape /metrics: metrics basic-auth credentials or the allowed-networks list drift out of sync with the Prometheus scrape config, or the scrape target's network path breaks. Every alertable entry in this document that depends on this endpoint goes dark silently -- Prometheus reports a missing series rather than an explicit error to the operator.

payload_or_id.title: Storage metrics collector stalled
payload_or_id.description: The in-process metrics-collector goroutine (GatherStorageMetrics) stops updating the storage-derived gauges (users, feeds, broken_feeds, entries, DB pool stats) because its query loop errors out repeatedly -- the gauges then report stale values indefinitely rather than an explicit gap, silently undermining every alert based on them.

payload_or_id.title: Elevated image-proxy failure rate
payload_or_id.description: An elevated rate of failures in the built-in image proxy that fetches external media on the browser's behalf -- entries show broken images in the reading view.

payload_or_id.title: Expired web session cleanup failure
payload_or_id.description: The periodic deletion of expired web sessions fails repeatedly, causing the sessions table to grow without bound over time.

payload_or_id.title: Old entry archiving failure
payload_or_id.description: The periodic archiving of old read/unread entries fails repeatedly, causing the entries table to grow without bound, which slowly degrades entry-list and search query performance for the whole instance over time.

payload_or_id.title: Orphan feed-icon cleanup failure
payload_or_id.description: The periodic deletion of feed icons no longer referenced by any feed fails repeatedly, causing the icons table to grow without bound.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Purely a slow disk-space/row-count growth concern with no functional or user-visible impact on any relevant timescale; better caught by generic database disk-usage alerting on the PostgreSQL host (outside this app's scope) than by a dedicated app-level signal.

payload_or_id.title: Interactive CLI admin command failure
payload_or_id.description: Any of the rare interactive admin commands (-create-admin, -reset-password, -flush-sessions, -export-user-feeds, -reset-feed-errors, -reset-feed-next-check-at) exits with an error, most commonly a database error.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Synchronous, operator-invoked, interactive commands: the exit code and stderr output return directly to the operator's terminal in the same moment the failure happens, a strictly faster and more precise feedback loop than any background alert could provide.

payload_or_id.title: dup probe
payload_or_id.description: dup

event.text:
All 27 failure modes were accepted in the batch (confirmed via duplicate-id rejection).

## Phase 2 — Failure Modes: submitted

I worked outward from each phase-1 component through its causal chain to the user-visible ends, then classified every entry's `coverage_status` now (required by the schema) so the alerting fate is explicit rather than deferred:

**Root/infrastructure causes (not user-visible themselves):** unhandled goroutine panic, OOM, startup-precondition failure, DB connection failure, DB pool exhaustion, outbound egress degraded, HTTP proxy unavailable, worker-pool saturation, metrics-collector stall — these are the early-detection points upstream of what users actually notice.

**User-visible ends, each with `caused_by` populated:** total outage, elevated 5xx/latency, per-request panics, auth-failure spikes, feed-refresh stalling/degrading, scraper/favicon/image-proxy/RSS-Bridge/integration failures.

**Coverage classification** (the phase's core deliverable per the "alert or reasoned exclusion" principle):
- **8 alertable** — an existing metric already covers it (e.g. `broken_feeds`, `background_feed_refresh_duration{status}`, DB pool gauges, and — notably — the Go client's auto-registered `process_resident_memory_bytes`/`go_memstats` for OOM risk).
- **12 metric-gap** — real, plausible failures with *no* current signal: notably the entire HTTP layer has zero per-request metrics (error rate, latency, recovered panics), and integrations/auth/image-proxy/egress have no counters at all. These become phase-3 recommendations.
- **7 excluded**, each with a stated reason — e.g. cosmetic-only (favicon), self-reporting-to-the-actor (RSS-Bridge discovery, interactive CLI admin commands), short-lived-process-invisible-to-pull-scraping (CLI batch jobs), or collapses-into-a-broader-alert (startup failures and panics fold into process-down; orphan-icon cleanup is better caught by host-level disk alerting).

One structural finding worth flagging: **`fm-metrics-scrape-failure`** — if Prometheus stops scraping `/metrics` (auth/network drift), every alertable entry above goes silently dark. It's alertable via Prometheus's own `up` metric, which is the standard meta-monitoring catch for this.

Ready for your review before phase 3 (metric coverage).

payload_or_id.rationale: No per-request HTTP metric exists at all today despite the process serving four distinct API surfaces (REST, web UI, Fever, Google Reader) plus health/metrics endpoints -- middleware.go only writes a slog.Debug line per request. A single labeled histogram at the shared middleware layer gives error-rate, latency-percentile, and (once the middleware also wraps handlers in its own recover()) panic-count observability in one place, without needing three separate metrics.
payload_or_id.details: Add a histogram `miniflux_http_request_duration_seconds{route,method,status_class}` observed in internal/http/server/middleware.go's middleware() wrapper: `route` is the matched ServeMux pattern (not the raw path, to bound cardinality against numeric IDs), `status_class` is one of 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx/panic. Wrap the call to `next.ServeHTTP` in a deferred recover() that records status_class="panic", re-logs, and returns a 500 -- this also closes the gap where a recovered handler panic currently only reaches net/http's own error log.

payload_or_id.rationale: No login/authentication outcome is counted anywhere today (form login, API key, HTTP basic auth for Fever/Google-Reader/metrics, OAuth2/OIDC, WebAuthn all just return an error to the caller). A systemic spike -- as opposed to the expected background rate of typos and expired credentials -- is only detectable with a labeled counter.

payload_or_id.rationale: Feed fetch, content scraping, favicon fetch, subscription/RSS-Bridge discovery, and the image proxy all funnel through the same internal/reader/fetcher.RequestBuilder/ResponseHandler choke point, but no metric is recorded there today (only feed-refresh and scraper durations are recorded, two layers up, with no way to isolate a proxy-specific failure or the image-proxy path at all). One counter at this shared layer distinguishes a general egress outage from a proxy-specific one and adds coverage for the image proxy, which currently has no signal whatsoever.
payload_or_id.details: Add a counter `miniflux_outbound_fetch_total{purpose,via_proxy,status_class}` incremented wherever `fetcher.NewResponseHandler(...)` is consulted (internal/reader/handler, internal/reader/subscription/finder.go, internal/reader/icon/checker.go, internal/reader/scraper/scraper.go, internal/ui/proxy.go's mediaProxy). `purpose` in {feed,scraper,favicon,subscription_discovery,image_proxy}, `via_proxy` bool, `status_class` in {ok,http_error,network_error,rate_limited}.

## Phase 3 — Metric Coverage: submitted

**Metrics inventory (16 entries):** all 13 app-defined Prometheus metrics from `internal/metric/metric.go` (feed-refresh/scraper/archive-duration histograms, users/feeds/broken_feeds/entries gauges, 7 DB-pool gauges), tied to their exact definition and observation call sites. Plus 3 auto-registered Go-client metrics (`process_resident_memory_bytes`, `go_memstats_alloc_bytes`, `go_goroutines`) that I'd relied on in phase 2 for OOM detection — included with a note that they're registered implicitly by the Prometheus client library's `init()`, not by application code, but are genuinely exposed at `/metrics`.

**Coverage status resolved for all 27 failure modes:**
- **8 alertable** — confirmed against the actual inventory: existing histograms/gauges suffice (e.g. `broken_feeds` + `background_feed_refresh_duration{status}` for feed-fetch spikes, DB-pool gauges for exhaustion, the Go-client memory/goroutine gauges for OOM). Two of these (`fm-daemon-process-down`, `fm-metrics-scrape-failure`) have no app-emitted detecting metric — they rely on Prometheus's own scrape-`up` signal, which needs no code change, so they stay alertable with an empty `detecting_metric_ids`.
- **12 metric-gap** — confirmed real: I verified the HTTP layer has *zero* per-request instrumentation, and auth/egress/integrations/scheduler-liveness/worker-pool/collector-heartbeat/session-cleanup have no signal at all.
- **7 excluded** — unchanged from phase 2, no new metric needed.

**8 new metric recommendations** cover all 12 gaps, several deliberately consolidating multiple failure modes onto one instrumentation point where the code already funnels through a shared choke point (e.g. one `miniflux_http_request_duration_seconds{route,method,status_class}` histogram at the shared middleware covers error-rate, latency, *and* recovered panics; one `miniflux_outbound_fetch_total` counter at the shared `fetcher.RequestBuilder` layer covers egress-degradation, proxy failures, and the previously-uninstrumented image proxy).

No amendment to phase 2 was needed — the coverage_status values set then already matched this deeper inventory pass.

Ready for your review before phase 4 (alert recommendations).

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert
serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode
may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).

annotations.summary: Miniflux is not responding to Prometheus scrapes
annotations.description: The miniflux scrape target has been unreachable for 2 minutes. This is either a total outage (process crashed, failed to start, or hung) or the /metrics endpoint specifically has become unreachable (auth/allowed-networks drift, network path break) -- both look identical to Prometheus. Check process liveness first (container/orchestrator status), then the metrics endpoint's basic-auth and allowed-networks configuration if the process itself is otherwise serving traffic.

annotations.summary: Miniflux memory or goroutine count is growing on a trajectory toward exhaustion
annotations.description: Resident memory is projected to grow by more than 50% in the next hour, or the goroutine count is projected to more than double -- both are leading indicators of an OOM kill or runtime allocation failure before it happens. Investigate for a stuck goroutine leak (e.g. a hung feed fetch) or an unusually large batch of concurrently refreshing feeds.

annotations.summary: Miniflux appears unable to connect to PostgreSQL
annotations.description: The database connection pool has dropped to zero open connections, or both feed-refresh and entry-archiving are failing simultaneously -- the two independent background paths that both hit the database. Check PostgreSQL reachability, credentials, and connection limits.

annotations.summary: Miniflux database connection pool is under pressure
annotations.description: Requests are waiting for a free database connection, or the pool is running at over 90% utilization. Check for a slow-query regression, a load spike, or DATABASE_MAX_CONNS set too low for current concurrency.

annotations.summary: Miniflux HTTP error rate is elevated
annotations.description: More than 5% of requests across the REST API, web UI, Fever API, and Google Reader API are failing with a 5xx status or a recovered handler panic. Requires the mr-http-request-duration-histogram metric (not yet implemented) to be wired up. Check for a database issue (see the DB alerts) or a recent deploy introducing a handler bug.

annotations.summary: Miniflux p95 HTTP request latency is elevated
annotations.description: The 95th percentile request duration across all HTTP entrypoints has exceeded 2 seconds for 10 minutes. Requires the mr-http-request-duration-histogram metric (not yet implemented) to be wired up. Check database pool saturation first.

annotations.summary: Miniflux authentication failure rate is elevated
annotations.description: Over 30% of login attempts across all methods (form, API key, basic, OAuth2/OIDC, WebAuthn) are failing. Requires the mr-authentication-attempts-counter metric (not yet implemented). Check for a bad deploy affecting credential verification or a DB issue on the users table.

annotations.summary: Miniflux outbound fetches are failing broadly
annotations.description: Over half of all outbound requests (feed fetch, scraping, favicons, integrations, RSS-Bridge, image proxy) are failing. Requires the mr-outbound-fetch-outcome-counter metric (not yet implemented). Check DNS resolution and egress network/firewall path from the host.

annotations.summary: Miniflux's configured outbound proxy is failing requests
annotations.description: Over half of requests routed through the configured HTTP/SOCKS proxy (or rotation pool) are failing, while overall egress may otherwise be healthy. Requires the mr-outbound-fetch-outcome-counter metric (not yet implemented). Check the proxy's own health and credentials.

annotations.summary: Miniflux image proxy failure rate is elevated
annotations.description: Over 30% of image-proxy requests (fetching external media on the browser's behalf) are failing. Requires the mr-outbound-fetch-outcome-counter metric (not yet implemented). Users will see broken images in the reading view.

annotations.summary: Miniflux feed-refresh failure rate is elevated
annotations.description: Over 20% of all feeds are currently broken, or over 30% of refresh attempts in the last 15 minutes have failed -- beyond the normal background rate of individually dead/misconfigured feeds. Check for a systemic egress issue or a parser regression after a recent deploy.

annotations.summary: Miniflux feed refresh has stopped making progress
annotations.description: The scheduler tick heartbeat is stale, or jobs are queued with zero completions in 15 minutes -- feed refresh has stopped entirely, not just degraded. Requires the mr-scheduler-heartbeat-gauge and mr-worker-pool-queue-depth-gauge metrics (not yet implemented). Check for a deadlocked worker pool or a scheduler goroutine that has exited.

The feed-refresh job queue depth is above 20 and trending upward -- the worker pool is saturated, likely by slow-responding feed sources or scraper targets. Requires the mr-worker-pool-queue-depth-gauge metric (not yet implemented).

annotations.summary: Miniflux content-scraper failure rate is elevated
annotations.description: Over 30% of full-content scrape requests (crawler-mode feeds) are failing in the last 15 minutes. Entries fall back to the short feed summary. Check for a systemic egress issue.

annotations.summary: Miniflux third-party integration push failure rate is elevated for one or more providers
annotations.description: Over half of entry pushes to at least one configured third-party integration provider are failing in the last 15 minutes. Requires the mr-integration-push-outcome-counter metric (not yet implemented). Check that provider's status page, then this instance's integration credentials.

annotations.summary: Miniflux's storage metrics collector has stopped updating
annotations.description: The storage-derived gauges (users, feeds, broken_feeds, entries, DB pool stats) have not refreshed in over 15 minutes -- every alert built on them may be looking at stale data. Requires the mr-metrics-collector-heartbeat-gauge metric (not yet implemented).

The periodic deletion of expired web sessions has failed at least once in the last day. Requires the mr-session-cleanup-outcome-metric metric (not yet implemented). Left unaddressed, the sessions table grows without bound.
The periodic archiving of old read/unread entries has failed at least once in the last day. Left unaddressed, the entries table grows without bound and query performance degrades over time.

## Phase 4 — Alert Recommendations: submitted

**18 alert recommendations**, each a valid PromQL `AlertRuleInput` (name, expr, for_duration, severity, annotations with summary+description), covering all **20 non-excluded failure modes** — none left unmapped:

- **Two-fm consolidations**, each taking the higher severity per the stated rule:
  - `ar-scrape-target-down` (`up{job="miniflux"}==0`) serves both `fm-daemon-process-down` and `fm-metrics-scrape-failure` — from Prometheus's perspective these two are the same observable signal, so one alert legitimately covers both.
  - `ar-http-5xx-error-rate` serves `fm-http-error-rate-spike` (critical) and `fm-http-handler-panic-recovered` (warning) → alert takes **critical**.
- **8 alerts against already-implemented metrics** (the phase-3 "alertable" set): scrape-down, OOM/goroutine-growth via `predict_linear`, DB connection/pool health, feed-fetch error rate, scraper error rate, entry-archiving failure.
- **10 alerts against the phase-3 metric recommendations** (not yet implemented) — each annotation explicitly names the `mr-*` id it depends on, so it's clear these need the instrumentation landed first: HTTP error-rate/latency, auth-failure rate, egress/proxy/image-proxy errors, scheduler-stall, worker-backlog, integration-push failures, metrics-collector staleness, session-cleanup failures.

I also filled in the `coverage.yaml` alert-side linkage (`alert_ids`) for all 20 failure modes, mirroring the metric-side linkage from phase 3, so the coverage record is fully mechanical and traceable end-to-end: failure mode → detecting/recommended metric → alert rule.

This closes the loop from phase 2's first principle: every failure mode now terminates in either an alert recommendation (20) or a reasoned exclusion (7) — 27 of 27 accounted for.

That's all four phases of the analysis. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to any alert thresholds/expressions, or want me to revisit the "excluded" calls now that the full chain is visible.
